utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber, first of all, establishes that Mr. Mladic is not present in the courtroom today. He has waived his right to attend a meeting, and his written confirmation of his waiver was filed yesterday. Therefore, we'll continue in his absence. No preliminaries were announced, which means that we could now proceed with the cross-examination of Mr. Hanson. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for the witness, Your Honour, I would say that my rough estimate is about one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that in the absence of Mr. Mladic, that we go back to the usual schedule, which is one hour and a half and have two breaks, rather than three times one hour and three breaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's fine with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll proceed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hanson, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Lukic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I'm having trouble hearing you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I may be listening to the Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if the usher could assist and put you on the right channel, which should be channel 4. Can you hear me now in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Lukic, if you're ready, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have your work in front of you?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the page 61 in English version, I think, and 65 in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this is P7431.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are there, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hanson, there's a table on this page signed on the 6th of May, 2014. Under approvals, we see the name of Mr. Thomas Parsons, as well as of Mr. Andreas Kleiser. We can see that Mr. Kleiser is the director of policy and co-operation. Please explain to us why was it necessary for Mr. Kleiser to approve your report.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Director Kleiser checks and approves all reports issued by ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One of my colleagues drew my attention to the issue of policy which is apparently some cause of -- cause of some confusion. What does actually director of policy and co-operation do in the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you should address to Director Kleiser for his exact job role, but one of his tasks is to control and check documentation emanating from ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who he reports to?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the director-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] And that is?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kathryne Bomberger.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And where is she seated?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where is she seated, where is his office?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In ICMP headquarters, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please tell us, if you know, what is Mr. Kleiser's profession?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a lawyer, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know why would a lawyer need to approve your product, your work?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. ICMP's documentation policy states all reports will be checked and approved. And for these reports, scientific reports, both Thomas Parsons and Andreas Kleiser check and approve. For these reports that I produce, so excavation reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could we go to the concrete level rather than to stay in the abstract level. I take it that the core issue is whether any influence was exercised by one of these persons. Could you tell us, did you submit a draft and were any changes suggested by the persons who approved your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thomas Parsons suggested changes to and amendments to text as my director.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps we move to that, because, Mr. Lukic, I think that's the relevant issue. Perhaps you could wait for further questions, but Mr. Lukic may be interested in what kind of changes he may have suggested. And do I understand your last answer to be that Mr. Kleiser did not suggest any changes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my recollection, Your Honour, he did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please tell us, then, what sort of changes did Mr. Parsons request of you.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some grammatical changes, typos, and clarifications of grammar and technical terms so that he had a clear understanding of the report content and meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he intervene in the gist of your work? Did he require any such changes?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hanson, do you recall another paper of yours entitled, [In English] and I will quote the title. It's: How to do forensic archaeology under the auspices of large organisations like the UN.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do. That's a published chapter in a book.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will quote one sentence and ask you something about that sentence. And if you want, it's not in our system, but it says: "At the very worst, the evidence itself might become prejudiced by dissident team members writing letters of denigration that fall into the hands of the defence." Do you remember this sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we have a page number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not from this work. It's the other paper written by Mr. Hanson and he just confirmed that he remembers it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you disclosed a copy to Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because one sentence, I don't know how long that contribution is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's 18 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think it would be fair that Mr. Tieger has an opportunity to look at the context in which it was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fairness, I have what I believe is a copy of that in front of me. I'm just looking at the moment for a page reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's page number 2, paragraph number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber doesn't have it, but please proceed for the time being, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I should note it's -- it has been uploaded as 1D5491.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, perhaps, irrespective of whether you'll tender it or not, that we have it on our screens already --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. So can we have 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we have it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you switch off your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 2, paragraph 2. Can we all see it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hanson, why would you instruct that some things should be hidden from the defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What? That is a very unfair question under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- could you please quote exactly what you want to put to the witness and then ask a question in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, third line, it says: "At the very worst, the evidence itself might become prejudiced by dissident team members writing letters of denigration that fall into the hands of the defence." My understanding of this sentence is that something should not fall into the hands of the defence. Is it what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This line, this paragraph is written by my co-author, but I believe the gist of the meaning is that information from different sources going to defence may affect or prejudice evidence, not that anything would be withheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you said your co-author. How did you understand this sentence then?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness said a minute ago: It's the text of the co-author, but this is how I understand what he means. That's his understanding, therefore. Please put your next question to the witness, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, is the meaning of this text that some things should be prevented from falling into the hands of the defence?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, in your view, this sentence would then mean that things should be provided or can be provided to the defence.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Will be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe if I can just ask one question. Mr. Hanson, based on the wording of the sentence, would it not be any prejudice -- would there be no prejudice if that kind of information fell into the hands of the prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prejudice in terms to the evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At the very worst, the evidence might be prejudiced. So would the evidence not be prejudiced if that kind of information fell into the hands of the prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the sentence does not say the evidence would have been prejudiced if it fell into the hands of the parties. It says "the hands of the defence." Now one of the parties is the prosecution. I'm asking would the same effect not arise if it fell into the hands of the prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the word "parties" should have been the word used here. Is that what I understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that would be a better way of phrasing the sentence, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Back to my question. Do I understand you to be saying that the same prejudice would arise if it fell into the hands of the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, evidence could be affected for all parties, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hanson, however, you always see yourselves in the role of someone working for the prosecution; correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, we do not work for the prosecution. We provide assistance to prosecutors, among other authorities. In Bosnia, we are assisting the Bosnian government and, through one of their vehicles, the prosecutor's office whom we have much interaction with, but we not working for them. We are assisting the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's see what the last paragraph on this page has to say about that. [In English] It says: "None of our comments is intended to devaluate the role of other forensic professionals. However, we disagree with Snow's opinion that a forensic anthropologist can practice forensic archaeological work after reading a few articles and perhaps attending a summer school ... more experience than this is required to evaluate what went on at mass grave and to bring work to a successful completion. Furthermore, it is dangerous for the prosecution to present an anthropologist as an expert witness about mass graves when the defence may call a stratigraphically experienced archaeologist." So is it true that actually here you expressed that you are on a prosecution side and the danger is coming from the defence?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, there's no expression there that we are working for the prosecution. We provide an opinion about expert witnesses for -- that might be used by prosecution and defence from the experience that we've had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you said, "Furthermore, it is dangerous for the prosecution," did you mean for the parties then again? Is it again misstated?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, for the prosecution, and we go on to say -- make a comment about what the defence may do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question by Mr. Lukic was whether in the opposite sequence, that is, to present such evidence by -- that the defence would present such evidence and then the prosecution would call such another expert, whether that would be similarly dangerous.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your comment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the text says if the -- it's dangerous for the prosecution to present, I would say, evidence which is not of good quality, that's how I understand it, because the defence would then present counterevidence to that. Now, the question was whether this is just limited to the prosecution doing this, or would the same be true if the defence would present evidence which can be easily or at least can be contradicted by experts from the other party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this example we describe once in our -- yes, you could expand that sentence and provide another example where prosecution, defence are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Or possibly use different language as to say: "Furthermore, it is dangerous for a party to present an anthropologist as an expert witness about mass graves when the opposite party may call ..." That would be more elegant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think that would be a more elegant sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, the -- we look at this contribution. Was this inspired by any existing conflict of views in a specific situation or is it just presented as a general explanation of your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's a general explanation from work drawn across many examples, personal work and other examples from -- that we know of or we've discussed at conferences or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence, Your Honour. We need only two pages. Maybe we could only reserve the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We reserve the number and then you take it upon you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just first and second page, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to upload the two selected pages, inform Mr. Registrar about the number under which they're uploaded, and then we'll decide on admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, will the two pages include the first page?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, only to know which the document is in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number to be reserved for it would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will be D1084, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, there would be no objections against admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, other than reserving the opportunity to consider whether remaining parts of the article shed light on the submitted two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, to further contextualise. Therefore, these two pages will be admitted once uploaded and Mr. Tieger could we hear from you within the next 48 hours whether you would wish do add anything to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You now -- where you intended to switch off, you switched on your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My fingers are apparently not co-ordinating so well with the equipment today. My response was: Yes, that's a generous period of time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to have on our screens 1D1123, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hanson, we see Mr. Odobasic's statement in front of us which he provided to the OTP of this Tribunal in 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before I forget and before we continue, the document of which you'll upload two pages, is there a B/C/S translation of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, there is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's not. Does the Defence refrain from requiring a B/C/S translation in this context?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The problem is that we cannot ask for B/C/S translation officially. That's what we were informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But therefore I asked you whether you would be satisfied if we would receive this evidence without a B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would be satisfied just to have it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then exceptionally the Chamber will consider to admit this evidence even without a B/C/S translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hanson, are you aware of the objections to the work of the ICMP made by Mr. Odobasic?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not. I haven't seen this statement before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Today and yesterday, you spoke about the excavations -- or exhumations in Jakarina Kosa and that was also part of your work --

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sorry to interrupt, but that was not part of my work. I've never worked at Jakarina Kosa.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Maybe it was not translated. I said it was part of your work, meaning your -- the document you provided as a contextual part.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need page 2, and, actually, it's page -- 2 or 3. In B/C/S, it's 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In English, give me one second. Page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Odobasic states in paragraph 1 here that he was providing the statement in a private capacity and not as the deputy of Mr. Amor Masovic who is the chairman of the B and H Federal Commission for Tracing Missing Persons. At the time, we know that Mr. Odobasic was Amor Masovic's deputy. In paragraph 7, he states: "From 11th of September until 12th of October, 2001, the commission exhumed a mass grave at Jakarina Kosa linked to the Prijedor investigation. Investigator Nikolas Sebire from the OTP monitored the exhumation. 373 bodies were exhumed, and The Hague anthropologist Jose Baraybar and his team were in charge of the anthropological treatment of the bodies in the Sejkovaca hall in Sanski Most." Are you aware that in this report it's noted that there was a case in Jakarina Kosa where it was established that there were two bodies named for only one person?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this statement or read the report referred to, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you're not aware of this error reported in the report on Jakarina Kosa which you cited in your own report.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring here to where it states in paragraph 8: Report from the Bihac Cantonal Court number KR 1-55/01?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] That's, yeah, further in the statement of Mr. Odobasic, that's true. But I'm asking you whether you knew at the time when you addressed this report about this report in connection to Jakarina Kosa, did you know about this mistake in that report?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which report are you referring to? The one described here?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. The one quoted in your work.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not a report. That is a published article from a scientific journal by Baraybar and Gasior, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you use it to enter data into your own report relating to Jakarina Kosa or for any other purpose?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The published article?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I used that for background information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you rely on that when drawing your conclusions on the basis of what you yourself investigated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- that published article I used for background information for Jakarina Kosa which is why I provided it in my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But did you draw any personal conclusions on Jakarina Kosa or did you just refer to it as something that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simply a reference. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If -- would any mistakes in that, would that have had any influence on the conclusions you drew on the basis of your own work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I wasn't aware of any mistakes within that journal article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to my question but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not, no, is the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would not have influenced it if there were mistakes or not because you did not rely on it as a basis for your conclusions. It's just background information, if I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Background information, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you able to rule out today the existence of errors, such as this, relating to the report or the work in Tomasica?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Errors such as ... which ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That it was established that there were two bodies under one name. By the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure where the error is you were describing, two bodies under one name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that Eva Klonowski -- do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eva Klonowski, yes, sir, an anthropologist. Eva Klonowski.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who does Eva Klonowski work for?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not tell you who Eva Klonowski works for.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that she worked for the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand she was contracted to ICMP previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 15 of Mr. Odobasic's statement - this is page 5 in the B/C/S version and probably 4 in the English version - Mr. Odobasic stated that he knows or knew that Eva Klonowski made a mistake in establishing the sex of one of the victims. Do you have information that such errors did occur previously in the work of the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't -- I haven't any information about work on the Jakarina Kosa cases concerning Eva Klonowski. That was before my time working at the ICMP, and I haven't examined any of her work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that there were errors in establishing the identity of bodies, meaning that they were handed over to a family and then it was established that because they were wrongly identified, they had to be dug up again and given to a different family? This something that we can see in paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I don't have knowledge of this particular case stated, but the issue of misidentifications is not unusual and it's one that has been encountered by Missing Persons Institute and ICMP while reviewing cases in the mortuaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about the frequency of this happening, as far as you're aware of? Is it in 1 per cent, 10 per cent, 30 per cent, 0.1 per cent of the cases that you encounter such mistakes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The analysis and review of unidentified cases in the mortuaries, Your Honour, is an ongoing process now which ICMP is supporting. The classical method referred to in paragraph 16 in this document is what's -- the method of identification used which uses documents found on a body, clothing, personal effects, visual identification methods as opposed to DNA-led identification, and there are error rates in these classical methods when cases have been re-checked, using DNA. This has been published upon, I believe, at -- a paper in 2001. I couldn't quote the exact error rates. We know from re-exhumed examples and re-checked examples that it is a consistent problem and one that goes to the methods especially in the early years after the conflict of how bodies were identified. And it's the checking against DNA which is a very assured way of identification that is highlighting these issues. Unfortunately, there are misidentifications but they do occur and, in fact, in an ICMP stock-taking report of last year which we've provided to show the work of identification in Bosnia since 1996, one of our recommendations is that the misidentifications are addressed as fully as possible by Bosnia's authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you consider them to be the result of the flaws in the classical method, or do you consider it a clear lack of accuracy and -- so is it rather the system or is it the bad operations that would, in your view, explain these misidentifications? And, again, if you could give us any -- any raw figure, not precise, but are we talking about 1 per cent, are we talking about 30 per cent? Could you give us a little bit more, if you can, of course, on that issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the system is -- there are limits when anthropologists examine the remains to -- with certain cases where they can assess it is male or female accurately, especially if the remains are fragmented or damaged. Have in all mortuaries in Bosnia the anthropologists been available to look at all the cases and check them? No. Were a lot of cases identified in the early years through clothing and documents without additional checks of anthropology or DNA? Yes. And I understand from our published stock-taking there are 8.000 classical or traditionally identified cases in Bosnia which have been accounted for, identified using those methods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Without the backing of DNA -- without the backing of DNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Without the backing of DNA, Your Honour. I think the number of cases which have been DNA-identified is reaching around 15.000, but I'd refer to my director and colleague, Thomas Parsons, to provide you with accurate information as to the DNA identifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it from your answer that you're not in a position to further quantify the level of such errors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not able to quantify exactly, Your Honour. It does vary between sites, events. It's very difficult to identify people in secondary graves where the remains are co-mingled. It's more straightforward to identify people if they're graves that are undisturbed, the bodies are whole. It does depend on the circumstances. So from our experience, and this is an ongoing process, the error rate varies very much between location and between event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that there were cases of a body of a person being identified, it's handed over to the family, the family buries the body, but then the body of that person is subsequently exhumed at a completely different location?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is not an uncommon occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am afraid I do not fully understand the answer, perhaps also not the gist of the question. Is it that the body is then moved to another grave or is it actually establishing that it could not have been the body they thought they would have buried because that body then later appears somewhere else? I'm just trying to understand both question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I understood the question to mean the person was positively identified later because they were exhumed in another place. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I understand both question and answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Mr. Vehid Sljivar is?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at page 6 in the B/C/S, please. And I think we see it on the screen already in the English version. We're going to be looking at paragraph 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph, paragraph 24, Roman VIII, Mr. Odobasic states the following: "In order to hide all those pieces of information regarding wrong identification, Mr. Vehid Sljivar, as an active police officer with the cantonal MUP Bihac, was receiving a 500 convertible mark bribe every month from the ICMP. This is a copy of an ICMP letter recommending that he be hired by the ICMP. His police commissioner, Husein Jakupovic, confirmed this to me. Sljivar is most probably still receiving this bribe. He is still employed with the MUP Bihac and at the same time he is on the payroll of the ICMP." Do you have any personal knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. No, I've never heard of this or I've never read this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then, under item IX, we can see that Mr. Sljivar gave -- Mr. Odobasic gave a copy of this letter to the cantonal prosecutor in Bihac. And then under Roman IX, it says: "This is a copy of a letter I sent to the cantonal prosecutor in Bihac, Mr. Asim Dzafic, in March 2005. The letter is self-explanatory and is referring also to above-named police inspector Vehid Sljivar and the covering up of DNA reports."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the underlying documents, do you have them? Because to say -- to present to this witness and to this Chamber evidence saying this letter, number IX, is self-explanatory without knowing what that letter is, makes it more difficult for us to assess the probative value of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will -- we will certainly ask to receive the documents the Prosecution received from Mr. Odobasic and we will be able to provide Your Honours with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've not asked it yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I have received no such request. I only saw this on the notification, this particular document on the notification sent to us after -- immediately after the cross-examination commenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But we will -- I hope we will be able to acquire those documents from the Prosecution and we will tender them through the bar table. Or maybe through the next Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hanson, do you have any knowledge about bribes by the ICMP to policemen so that they would conceal evidence and data?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The witness's answer pre-empts the genuine need for any intervention but that would otherwise have not been a fair characterisation of what information had been previously posed to the witness in the context of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose that the objection is moot at this moment, so can I move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't consider it to be an objection but, rather, a comment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know who Nermin Sarajlic is, Mr. Hanson?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pathologist of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And do you know that he worked together with Eva Klonowski during the period that Mr. Odobasic is talking about and that together with Eva Klonowski he took the samples from the bodies for analysis?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Jakarina Kosa --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- site? Yes, I understand that they worked at the excavation. I do not have details about the examination and sampling and who undertook those.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. [Interpretation] And did you know that Mr. Odobasic contacted the ICMP directly, pointing to the errors that he presents here in his statement?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we shortly see paragraph 28, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm actually going to start with paragraph 27, which states: "One of the bigger mistakes during the Bosanska Krajina exhumation was that ICMP handed over the Sejkovaca hall with 1.000 bodies to one incompetent physician who had never worked on such jobs. This was Eva Klonowski's assistant, Nermin Sarajlic. He is the man who never did one single independent autopsy or exhumation." Are you aware of the work experience of Mr. Sarajlic during that period?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is before my time at ICMP. I wasn't in Bosnia during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 28, Mr. Odobasic states: "A similar letter as the one sent to the Bihac prosecutor I also sent to Kathryne Bomberger, chief of the ICMP, who said that Nermin was the least competent physician with the ICMP." Did you ever discuss the professional qualifications of Mr. Sarajlic with Kathryne Bomberger?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not discussed with Kathryne Bomberger Nermin Sarajlic's competence or professional work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 30 and 31, Mr. Odobasic speaks about Ana Boza, and he asserts that Ana Boza was removed from the process, from the process of identification and autopsies, because the ICMP wanted to hide the mistakes made at Kevljani previously by Eva Klonowski and Nermin Sarajlic because Ana Boza would draw attention to those mistakes. Do you have any information in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I've never heard of this before. I've never read this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And are you aware, is it usual, that a person who conducts the autopsies also does the final identification of the victims?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it usual?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Is it usual, yes.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the court-appointed pathologist is under court order to complete and finalise and finish a case unless prosecutor deems otherwise, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give me one second. [Interpretation] I have just one other topic to cover with you, Mr. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. The paragraph you've shown, paragraph 30, would I be able to point one thing out? Because you asked if someone undertaking autopsy would complete the case. It says in paragraph 30, physician Ana Boza. I understand she was an anthropologist, so she was not a state-legislated pathologist, so as an anthropologist that does not complete identifications. I just thought that -- for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And Eva Klonowski, what is his occupation?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand, an anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Anthropologist. So is it usual that one is replaced by another so ... physician by anthropologist?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since Eva Klonowski replaced Ana Boza according to this statement?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't comment on this particular case, no. Do professionals get replaced? If deemed necessary by authorities, I'm sure it happens, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But both of them are anthropologists.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are both anthropologists, Your Honour, as far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I don't understand, Mr. Lukic, when you say "replacing a physician by an anthropologist," because these two are both anthropologists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's from the previous answer: "It says in paragraph 30, physician Ana Boza" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but if you look at transcript page 25, line 21: "Anthropologist. So it is usual that one is replaced by another, so a physician by anthropologist?" Is that what you meant to say or was it a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My understanding was that they are of the same occupation so that's how Mrs. Boza was able to be replaced with Eva Klonowski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's precisely my position and that's why I'm asking why you give them different professions here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because Mr. Hanson drew my attention that somewhere in paragraph 30 and it's in line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Line 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Line 7, page 25, line 14, page 25, I cannot fight this transcript. It's moving although I stopped it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Move on if you don't have the answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps since you are thinking about the next question. Do I now finally understand that Ana Boza was a physician, not an anthropologist, and that she was replaced by Eva Klonowski and Nermin Sarajlic, both being anthropologists? Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Ana Boza, as I understand, is an anthropologist; Eva Klonowski, an anthropologist; Nermin Sarajlic is a court-appointed pathologist in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so the information here is pretty much confusing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hanson, we get to our last topic that was discussed with you yesterday, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And before we move on, I think part of the answer of the witness is missing at page 27, line 7. So that needs perhaps special attention when working on the transcript because the -- Mr. Sarajlic, which was part of your answer, is not referred to here. And you said Mr. Sarajlic was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Court-appointed pathologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Court-appointed pathologist. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And to add something to this confusion, in page 27, line 5, the first word was not said by the Presiding Judge. Was a physician not an anthropologist. The word "pathologist" is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's now move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 119 of your report, you discussed the nature of clothing and you were asked about it yesterday by the Prosecution. You said that you found only civilian clothes items. I wanted to ask you about weapons first. While working in the field in Bosnia, did you find it common to find former fighters buried alongside their weapons? Did you ever have such a case?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How often were people buried with their weapons and where did you come across such cases?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: While working with the Banja Luka MPI office on a site on Mount Ozren, combatants were recovered who had munitions in military pouches. There were similar examples. So combatants are recovered with munitions, grenades, ammunition, yes. It's a regular occurrence. It happens every year, I think, as a general level of occurrence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was about weapons. Your answer is about munitions, grenades. Of course, you could consider them to be weapons, but any rifles or pistols?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fire-arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fire-arms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fire-arms have been encountered, I believe, in exhumations and excavations, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And weapons. It's not common to find fire-arms such as rifles or machine-guns buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, did you ever deal with the issue of how many members of the Muslim forces at the beginning of 1992 actually had uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Falls this within the competence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If he dealt with it, I -- that was my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If he has any knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, could you tell us whether you have any knowledge, and if so, on what basis you have that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge as to the issue of how many members of Muslim forces at the beginning of conflict had uniforms, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hanson, that was all we had for you at this moment. Thank you for answering our questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Tieger, we're at the time of a break, I think. How much ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not yet at a point of a break. Mr. Tieger, how much could you -- do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President. But if I understand correctly that the next break is actually at 11.00, I'll finish well before then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please continue then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked by Mr. Lukic about the anthropologically based assessment of the minimum number of individuals of 298 in Jakarina Kosa, a matter that was raised again this morning, beginning at LiveNote page 14, asked -- and then you were asked about the DNA-matching efforts demonstrating linkages between Tomasica and Jakarina Kosa, and you were further asked about ICMP's role and whether the ICMP labs in 2001 had required certifications. That was all at transcript pages 36307 through 308. Just a couple of questions in connection with that. First of all, do anthropologically based assessments of the minimum number of individuals generally result in the same number, a lower number, or a higher number of individuals when those remains are checked via the DNA process?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's unusual that it's the same number simply because in so many events and excavations, bodies are recovered not only as bodies but body parts, single bones. So the number of cases and the anthropological assessment to get a minimum number of individuals is not usually the same as the total number of DNA profiles that are found to be present when those remains are sampled. This can be because DNA cannot be extracted from some smaller fragmented bones, cases that are separate DNA matches together, so you may have DNA matches of several cases which belong to one individual, so you can get a lower number of DNA profiles. Sometimes you can get a higher number of DNA profiles than the minimum number of individuals estimated by anthropological assessment. It's scenario dependant. It's often not the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the process of the effort to determine any linkages between the remains found at Tomasica and those at Jakarina Kosa, would the ICMP have conducted or attempted DNA matches on all of the recovered remains from Jakarina Kosa to make that comparison?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's been undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So those could be checked in connection with the accuracy of the anthropologically based MNI; correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic has already indicated he intends to raise that further with -- apparently with Mr. Parsons or another witness, so I'll defer further questions on that until that time. Next, you were asked by Mr. Lukic, at transcript page 36321 and there was a follow up by the Bench on the next page, about whether there was evidence of an intention to remove the whole grave at Jakarina Kosa or only the portion actually robbed. I wanted to ask you if it's common or uncommon, if you know, to -- to find mass graves that have been only partially robbed and in which bodies and body parts still remain, notwithstanding the portion that had been disturbed and robbed?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is very common to find this. And in fact, in all the years of my work, I have never encountered a mass grave where all remains have been removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Hanson, there was some discussion this morning about whether you allegedly saw your role as working for the Prosecution in view of the -- of a comment in your article regarding excavations. Just to put that comment or those comments in context, has ICMP or have you ever been asked by a defence team to conduct an investigation of -- an excavation of a mass grave?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excavation of a mass grave, no. I have been asked and consulted for a defence team concerning death of multiple victims by burning, and concerning a civil case with disturbance to an -- an alleged unlawful disturbance of a cemetery. So I have worked with defence as a consultant to private expert matters in excavation and burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's all I had, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, have the questions in re-examination triggered any need for further --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- questions? Mr. Hanson, this therefore then concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions the parties have put to you and the Bench has put to you. And before I wish you a safe return home again, I'll first see whether Mr. Tieger, who is on his feet, his microphone activated, whether he is an obstacle to releasing you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's only the matter of tendering MFI P7431 into evidence and I thought that should be done before the witness leaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, the expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. P7431 is admitted into evidence. I now, Mr. Hanson, can release you. I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Rather than to have the next witness called, I would rather use the next six minutes to deliver a decision on behalf of the Chamber and then start with the examination of the next witness after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And before we leave, either now or just when you complete your remarks, I just wanted to add one matter regarding something Mr. Lukic had raised in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's start with that first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to the documents associated with the statement of Mr. Odobasic that Mr. Lukic said he would seek from the Prosecution, they've all been previously disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have the ERNs in front of me now if that's of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can give them to Mr. Lukic if he wishes to. Of course, it's a pity that they could not be included in the examination of the witness because then the Chamber would also have known what the documents were about on which Mr. Odobasic apparently has given his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, as I say, there was no obstacle that I can see in doing so. They had already been disclosed and -- along with the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, it would assist the Chamber if it would have had such documents available. We -- I'll now deliver a decision of the Chamber, a decision on the expertise of Dusan Dunjic, with regard to his analysis of Prosecution expert reports authored by several experts, including John Clark, Christopher Lawrence, and William Haglund. On the 30th of March of this year, the Defence filed a confidential notice of disclosure of Dusan Dunjic's expert report pursuant to 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Prosecution filed its notice pursuant to the same rule on the 24th of April, submitting that while it does not challenge the expert status of Dunjic or the relevance of his report, it does not accept the conclusions of his report and therefore wishes to cross-examine him. With respect to the applicable law concerning expert evidence, the Chamber recalls and refers to its 19th of October, 2012, decision concerning expert witness Richard Butler. On the basis of Dunjic's curriculum vitae and considering that the Prosecution does not dispute Dunjic's qualifications as a forensic expert, the Chamber is satisfied that he has specialised knowledge and expertise, and that such knowledge and expertise may be of assistance to the Chamber in assessing the expert evidence presented by the Prosecution during its case in-chief. With regard to the Prosecution's request to cross-examine the witness, the Chamber notes that the Defence plans to call Dunjic to give evidence. The Prosecution will therefore have the opportunity to cross-examine him. Based on the foregoing, the Chamber decides, pursuant to Rule 94 bis, that the Defence may call Dunjic to testify as an expert witness and that he shall be made available for cross-examination by the Prosecution. The Chamber defers its decision on the admission of the report to the time of the testimony. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. We have a few minutes left until 11.00. I'll use them to deal with two short items. I'd like to put the following schedule matters on the record. On the 12th of June of this year, following consultation with the parties and the Registry, the Chamber informed the parties that it would sit from Tuesday, the 7th of July, through Friday, the 10th of July, instead of 6 through 9 July. On the 17th of June, following consultation with the parties and the Registry, the Chamber informed the parties of a revised sitting schedule for Friday, the 10th of July. That day, we'll start at 11.30 and we'll have sittings until 1400 hours. We'll then recommence at 3.00 in the afternoon and adjourn at half past 5.00. Of course, the normal schedule for breaks in between sittings will be maintained. The Chamber is grateful for the co-operation of the parties and the Registry in this matter. This concludes the scheduling matter. Last item I will deal with, deals with the status of Exhibit P7198. On the 22nd of May, 2015, P7198, an intercept, was admitted into evidence and placed under seal. On the 22nd of June of this year, the Chamber informed the parties that it considers that the status of P7198 should be changed to public and invited them to submit their objections, if any, within two days. This can be found at transcript page 36162. The Chamber has not heard of any objections from the parties, and hereby, therefore, instructs the Registry to lift the confidential status of P7198. We take a break, and we resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, we are; Mr. Franjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Franjic, I assume. Before you give evidence, the rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Franjic. Please be seated. Mr. Franjic, you now can hear me in a language you understand, Mr. Franjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Franjic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Jeremy. You find him to your right. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Franjic.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could begin by you stating your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Bruno Franjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Franjic, what is your current professional position?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Head of the Department for Ballistics and Mechanoscopy at the Section for Ballistic and Mechanoscopic Expert Analysis, Forensic and IT Support Centre, Federal Police Administration, and I'm a Sarajevo court-sworn criminology expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Franjic, I'll ask you to perhaps speak a little bit more slowly just to ensure that your answer is fully captured on the record. Thank you. Now, sir, do you recall previously providing a copy of your CV to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 31101 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the document on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Do you recognise this to be your CV?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And does this detail your education, professional training, and professional experience?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, on this issue of past experience, could you very briefly inform the Court about your military experience during the war between 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: From the 6th of April, 1992, until the 6th of April, 1995, and then from the 6th of April until the 1st of October, 1995, and the 2nd of October, 1995, until the 20th of August, 1996, I was a member of the Croatian Defence Council in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 3 of the English of this document and page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, referring your attention to the section headed: "Membership," we read that -- that you've been the only -- that since September 2002, you've been the only representative of the countries of the former Yugoslavia who is a member of the Association of Fire-Arm and Tool Mark Examiners. Could you, again very briefly, explain to the Court what this association is.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: This is an association which has as its members experts who analyse traces of fire-arms and traces of tool marks. These experts come from over 50 countries of the world, and they are based in the United States, the association is based in the United States. First, I joined as a provisional member in 2002 and then from 2008 I became a permanent member. The only one from the countries of the former Yugoslavia. And I co-operate with all the members of the association, AFTE.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 31101 as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The Defence has no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7433, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, did you, at the request of the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina, prepare a report dated the 7th of May, 2014, that included ballistic analysis of certain shell casings and bullets?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the Court Officer please bring 65 ter 31093 to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recognise the document on the screen before you as the cover page of the report that we just referred to?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: I recognise it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, at this point I would propose to provide the witness with a colour hard copy of his report. Mr. Ivetic has seen a copy. I understand he has no objections to it being provided to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please seek the assistance of the usher to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- have it handed out to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 in the B/C/S and 3 in the English, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, on the screen before us, we see a page that in the middle part has subject: "Ballistic DNA and finger-print forensic analysis." Does your expertise cover all of these areas or just one?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Only some.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And is it the ballistic part of the report that your expertise covers?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And very briefly in relation to the DNA and finger-print analysis part of the report, can you recall whether the report reflects any useful findings in respect to that particular analysis?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: From what I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, below the subject header, we see a reference to an order for forensic analysis first dated the 14th of March, 2014, and another dated -- a supplemental order dated 7th of April, 2014. These orders were from whom?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: It was sent by the prosecutor of the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, towards the bottom of the English page and in the second paragraph in the page of the B/C/S, we read that it was ordered that a ballistic mechanoscopic - if we go to the next page in English, please - and other analysis be conducted of the cartridges and rounds found on the scene of the exhumation in the territory of Prijedor municipality, Tomasica mass grave, and the rounds found during the autopsy and examination of the bodies in the Sejkovaca KIP hall. And then we see a list of items below that. Now, sir, did you personally seize the items analysed in this report or were they provided to you by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: I did not find these objects. They were submitted to me along with orders for expert analysis issued by the B and H prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, below this, we see an itemised list of, firstly, cartridges and with an indication of where they were found and the marking given to them. And if we go to the next page, please, in each language, we see a reference to bullets fired and parts of bullets and where those bullets were found in the Sejkovaca morgue. And we see a reference to a date, and we see that they're linked to a particular body number. Now, all of this information, was that provided to you by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The information was given and presented in the expert report on the basis of what was cited in the requests for the expert analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And that request for the expert analysis came from, as you've already mentioned, the prosecutor of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 10 in the English and 6 in the B/C/S of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if we can focus on the bottom part of the page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, we see a reference to an order for forensic analysis and what that forensic analysis is aimed at establishing. Below that, we see a number of points. I'll just focus on two. The first is the -- that the analysis should establish the following: The calibre of the supplied cartridges and rounds and the type of weapon they were fired from; and, secondly, whether those -- the characteristics of those supplied rounds and cartridges match.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can skip forward to page 11, please, in the English and 6 in the B/C/S. Yeah, so we can stay on the same page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, we see a section headed "Findings" here. And perhaps we can go to the next page in the -- in each language, and, sir, while we are a doing that, if you could just very, very briefly give a overview of what this findings section contains.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: This is the ballistics expert analysis that is contained in this part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And this contains the details of the analysis that you conducted within the report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we'll shortly look at the opinion section in the report. Is that opinion section based on this -- these findings that you reflect here in this section of the report?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of analysis and findings, the final opinion is provided of the results of the expert analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Let's skip forward now to that final opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could go to page 102 in the English, please, and 64 in the B/C/S. If we could go to the bottom of the page in the B/C/S and immediately on the -- the preceding page in the English is a reference to opinion. I don't think we need to go to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And seeing this heading of -- now, sir, we read here about a number of matching shell casings there, their calibre, and the conclusion that you draw about the specific type of weapon that they were fired from. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Should we go to the top of the page in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, just the same page but to the top of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, on the basis of your previous answer, do I take it that you, in drawing the conclusions about the matches between the different cartridge casings, you provide more detailed reasons for the basis on which you make those findings in the findings section of your report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would for the record refer you to page 20 to 21 of the English and 14 to 15 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, throughout the report, there are references to disputed cartridges or bullets. What does "disputed" mean in the context of this report?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: In a ballistics analysis, a disputed bullet or a round is understood to be all traces, all bullets and rounds of unknown origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So these are the references to the bullets and the rounds that you were provided with and upon which you performed your analysis?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Disputed cartridges and disputed bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in just the B/C/S, please, and, sir, we see a reference here to three different clusters of cartridges and within each cluster you make your conclusion that they were fired by the same individual weapon. Now, we see the reference to firstly seven cartridges, then six cartridges and then five cartridges. Now combining these different cartridges, how many weapons did you conclude that those 18 cartridges were fired by?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: From seven different fire-arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now -- and we'll discuss those fire-arms shortly. But if we move on and we see the last point on this page refers to 50 disputed rounds, nine disputed pieces of round, and eight disputed bullet jackets, and 16 pieces of bullet jackets, and then they're itemised in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can skip forward to the end of this particular entry, which should be page 105 in the English and 66 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, in this section you refer to -- you refer to the bullets analysed, you refer to their calibre, and then towards the end of this paragraph, you draw a conclusion in relation to the class of fire-arms in which you think that these -- the bullets were fired. And the language that we read is that these bullets "could be" from bullets fired from and then you list the weapons. Now, with reference to this word "could be," to your knowledge and on the basis of your experience, are you aware of any other weapons that you think these bullets could have been fired in?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Based on many years of experience, I have been working as a ballistics expert for the past 18 years, I don't have any information that the disputed rounds or fragments of rounds could have originated from bullets fired from any other kind of fire-arm, other than those that are noted in the findings and the opinion of the expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now below this section, you refer to a handful of different calibre of bullets to the 7.62 by 39-millimetre bullets that you've just discussed in the last section, and you link certain pistols to those bullets that you identify. Now, below that, we see --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, please, in -- just in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: You basically list a series of bullets and parts thereof that were unsuitable for analysis. Now, combining the shell casings and the different calibre bullets that were suitable for analysis, how many different types of weapons did you conclude that those were used in?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: Judging by the cartridges, seven types of fire-arms were used of 7.62 by 39-millimetre, of that calibre. At least one fire-arm was of a pistol, 7.62 by 25-millimetres' calibre. Then there was a pistol of 7.62 millimetres. And there was one type of weapon, 7.7 by 57 millimetres' calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you've -- according to your analysis, what weapon was most frequently linked or what type of weapon was most frequently linked to the shell casings and the bullets that you were able to analyse?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC
utterances.text: The Kalashnikov automatic rifle or the Crvena Zastava automatic rifle, models M70 or light machine-gun M72, and semi-automatic rifle or the PAP produced by Crvena Zastava, M59/66. Its calibre is 7.62 by 39 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could go to page 110 in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could just intervene. We may want to check the answer to the last question. There was a weapon identified as 7.7 by 57 millimetre. I'm not sure that that is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7.62 times 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's in the prior question. It's line 7 of page 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- is that a line which starts with the pistol, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and then talks about a weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I -- I read to you and ask you to complete that answer. You said: "Then there was a pistol of 7.62 millimetres. And there was one type of weapon ..." And could you repeat what you referred to as the calibre of that one type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7.62 times 17 millimetres. 7.65, needs to be corrected, times 17. And 7.9 times 57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we could go to page 110 in the English, please, and the last page in the B/C/S of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
